title: Astronauts Return to Earth After 237 Days and 100 Million Miles in Space
summary:
Four astronauts are back on Earth after more than seven months living on the International Space Station. Their SpaceX capsule splashed down safely in the Pacific Ocean near Los Angeles on Thursday morning.

The Crew-12 team included NASA astronauts Jessica Meir and Jack Hathaway, European Space Agency astronaut Sophie Adenot and Russian cosmonaut Andrey Fedyaev. They launched on Feb. 13 and spent 237 days in orbit. During that time, they circled Earth more than 3,792 times and traveled over 100 million miles.

Recovery teams on special ships quickly reached the capsule and brought the crew aboard. After routine medical checks, the astronauts were set to travel to NASA's Johnson Space Center in Houston.

For Meir and Fedyaev, this was their second trip to space. For Hathaway and Adenot, it was their first.

The crew spent hundreds of hours on science experiments. One project explored ways to make stem cells in space, which could someday be used in medical treatments. Another tested a machine that makes IV fluids, the liquids doctors give patients through a tube, whenever they are needed. That could be very useful on long trips far from Earth. Other studies looked at nutrition in space and how blood flows in the body without gravity.

NASA says this research will help keep people healthy on future missions to the Moon and Mars.

Meir also made four spacewalks during the mission, bringing her career total to seven. That places her third among NASA women for the most spacewalks.

NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman thanked the crew and said building the ability to do missions like this again and again will help humans go farther.
why_it_matters: Learning how to keep astronauts healthy for months is a key step before people can safely travel to the Moon and Mars, and some of the research could also help medicine on Earth.

background_read: The International Space Station is a large laboratory that circles Earth, where astronauts from several countries live and work for months at a time.
Crews travel to and from the station in capsules, and SpaceX capsules return by splashing down in the ocean, where recovery ships pick them up.
Living without gravity changes the human body, so scientists study astronauts to learn how to keep people healthy on long trips.
NASA hopes to send people back to the Moon and later to Mars, which will require much longer missions than a stay on the station.
